planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into humus-rich, acidic woodland soil within reach of the roots of an existing tree or shrub, since buffalo nut is a root hemiparasite that establishes and grows far more vigorously with a living woody host nearby.

directions: Buffalo nut is a deciduous understory shrub of the sandalwood family, scattered through the shaded ravines and cove forests of the central and southern Appalachians from West Virginia south to Georgia and Alabama, often sharing the humus-rich, acidic duff beneath eastern hemlock and mixed hardwood canopy with galax and heartleaf. Its roots tap into the roots of a wide range of neighboring woody plants through haustoria, drawing supplemental water and nutrients while its own broad, dull green leaves continue to photosynthesize normally. Inconspicuous greenish flowers in spring are followed by a large, oily, pear-shaped drupe that gives the plant its common names; the oily kernel is mildly toxic and purgative to humans and is left alone by most wildlife. Site it near an established tree or shrub rather than in isolation, since seedlings and transplants struggle to thrive without a nearby root system to tap into.
